title: Greeting, Thanksgiving, and Assurance
content:
Paul opens by identifying himself as an apostle by God’s will and greets the church as those sanctified in Christ and called to be holy. He widens their horizon: they belong with all who call on Jesus everywhere. Grace and peace come from the Father and the Lord Jesus.
He thanks God that the Corinthians have been enriched in speech and knowledge, and that the gospel was confirmed among them. They do not lack any spiritual gift as they await Jesus’ return. Their future rests not on their performance but on God’s faithfulness: He will sustain them to the end so they will be blameless.
These opening verses both affirm and reorient the church. Even with their problems, they are God’s church, gifted by grace and upheld by a faithful Lord. Paul begins with gratitude and assurance before addressing corrections.
context_note: Before confronting divisions, Paul anchors the community in their shared calling and in God’s faithfulness. The rest of the chapter will correct their pride and factionalism by centering on Christ and His cross.
historical_note: Corinth was a wealthy, status-conscious port city. New believers there faced strong cultural pressure toward self-promotion and rhetorical showmanship.
original_language_note: Key terms: ekklēsia (church/assembly of God, v.2); hēgiasmenois (sanctified, v.2); charismati (gift, v.7); koinōnia (fellowship/participation with Christ, v.9).
jesus_connection: Jesus is the source of grace, the center of the church’s identity, and the faithful Lord who will keep His people blameless until His day.
apply_it:
- Where do you most need to remember that God is faithful to sustain you to the end?
- How does seeing yourself as “sanctified in Christ” shape your daily choices?
- In what ways can you thank God for gifts He has given your church?

title: A Call to Unity, Not Personalities
content:
Paul appeals for the Corinthians to agree and be united in mind and conviction. Reports from Chloe’s household reveal factions forming around favorite leaders—Paul, Apollos, Cephas, and even a group claiming Christ in a divisive way.
He exposes the absurdity: Christ is not divided, and no human leader was crucified for them. Paul is grateful he baptized few in Corinth, so no one can turn baptism into a badge of loyalty to him. Christ sent him to preach the gospel, not to build a fan club or impress with rhetorical flourish.
The cross loses its power when the church relies on human eloquence and personality cults. Unity comes from belonging to the crucified Christ, not aligning with celebrity leaders or preferred styles.
context_note: This section names the presenting problem—divisions—that the cross-centered wisdom of the next passage will correct. Later chapters (3–4) return to leadership and boasting.
historical_note: In Corinth, traveling teachers and sophists were prized for eloquence and status. Such cultural values likely fueled the Corinthians’ leader-based factions.
original_language_note: Schismata (divisions, v.10) highlights tears in the community. Kenōsē (emptied, v.17; from kenoō) warns against draining the cross of its power through self-exalting rhetoric.
jesus_connection: Jesus alone was crucified for us; allegiance belongs to Him. The cross, not charisma, gathers and unites the church.
apply_it:
- Are there subtle ways you attach your identity to a teacher, style, or tribe rather than to Christ?
- How can you pursue unity of conviction without uniformity of preference?
- What might it look like to make the cross—not eloquence or success—the measure of ministry?

title: The Cross and the Folly of Worldly Wisdom
content:
Paul contrasts two verdicts about the message of the cross: to those perishing, it is foolish; to those being saved, it is God’s power. He quotes Scripture to show God overturns human wisdom and strength.
Different groups seek different credentials—Jews demand miraculous signs, Greeks pursue philosophical sophistication—but the apostolic message is Christ crucified. This offends Jewish expectations and sounds absurd to Gentile wisdom, yet for the called, Christ is the very power and wisdom of God.
God’s way purposefully confounds boasting. What seems like divine “weakness” and “foolishness” at the cross proves stronger and wiser than anything humans can offer.
context_note: This is the theological center of the chapter. It explains why human-centered factions are incompatible with the gospel: the cross dismantles pride and resets all values.
historical_note: First-century Jews anticipated a Messiah marked by visible power; many Greeks prized rhetorical brilliance and philosophical coherence. A crucified Messiah cut against both expectations.
original_language_note: Logos tou staurou (word/message of the cross, v.18); sophia (wisdom, frequent); dynamis (power, v.24); skandalon (stumbling block, v.23).
jesus_connection: Jesus’ crucifixion is the decisive revelation of God’s saving power and wisdom. The gospel calls people not to admire human brilliance, but to trust the crucified and risen Christ.
apply_it:
- Where do you tend to measure power or wisdom by cultural standards rather than by the cross?
- How does Christ crucified reshape your view of success, weakness, and influence?
- Who might need to hear a simple, cross-centered word from you this week?

title: God’s Choice of the Lowly; Boast in the Lord
content:
Paul reminds the Corinthians of their beginnings: not many were wise, powerful, or noble by worldly measures. God deliberately chose the foolish, weak, and lowly to shame the strong, so that no one could boast before Him.
He centers everything on union with Christ: because of God, they are in Christ Jesus, who has become wisdom from God for them—righteousness, holiness, and redemption. All spiritual standing is a gift in Christ.
Therefore, the only fitting boast is in the Lord. This doxology dismantles pride in status, leaders, or achievements and redirects glory to God alone.
context_note: After exposing the emptiness of worldly wisdom, Paul shows how God’s calling of the unimpressive displays His grace. This prepares for later corrections about pride and gifts (chs. 3–4, 12–14).
original_language_note: Klesis (calling, v.26); katargēsē (nullify, v.28); dikaiosynē, hagiasmos, apolytrōsis (righteousness, holiness/sanctification, redemption, v.30).
jesus_connection: Jesus Himself is our wisdom and saving righteousness. Boasting ends because everything we need before God is found in Him.
apply_it:
- What parts of your story highlight God’s grace rather than your merit?
- How can you consciously “boast in the Lord” this week—in speech, prayer, or service?
- Which identities or achievements compete with Christ as the ground of your confidence?

title: Christ Crucified, Not Human Eloquence
content:
Paul reminds the church that when he first arrived, he did not rely on polished speech or philosophical flair. He narrowed his message to the heart of the gospel: Jesus Christ and Him crucified.
He admits coming in weakness, fear, and trembling—highlighting that the results in Corinth were not due to his charisma. Instead, the Spirit confirmed the message with power so their faith would rest on God’s power rather than human persuasion.
This protects the church from building on personalities or trends. The cross looks unimpressive to the world, but it is God’s power to save and the only solid foundation for enduring faith.
context_note: Following 1 Corinthians 1, where Paul contrasts God’s wisdom with human wisdom, this section shows how Paul’s ministry style matched his message. It sets up the following sections on true wisdom and spiritual discernment.
historical_note: Corinth prized impressive orators and traveling philosophers. By refusing to play that game, Paul undercut the city’s honor culture and redirected attention to Christ’s power.
original_language_note: “Demonstration” (Greek: apodeixis) suggests a clear showing or proof—here, the Spirit authenticating the preached word. “Wisdom” (sophia) signals the Greco-Roman ideal Paul deliberately relativizes in light of the cross.
jesus_connection: The passage centers on the crucified Christ as God’s saving power. Jesus’ cross is not an entry-level message but the essence of Christian wisdom and life.
apply_it:
- Where might you be tempted to rely on style, strength, or reputation instead of the simple truth of the cross?
- How have you seen the Spirit’s power, not your own, sustain faith in times of weakness?
- What might it look like to speak simply and clearly about Jesus this week?

title: God’s Hidden Wisdom Revealed by the Spirit
content:
Paul does speak wisdom—but not the short-lived wisdom of this age or its rulers. God’s wisdom was hidden and destined for believers’ glory before time began.
The rulers of this age did not recognize God’s plan; if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. What God prepared for those who love Him surpasses human imagination.
God reveals this hidden wisdom through the Holy Spirit. The Spirit opens up the deep things of God so that the church can grasp what could never be discovered by unaided human insight.
context_note: After rejecting showy rhetoric, Paul clarifies he is not anti-wisdom. He redefines wisdom as God’s eternal plan centered in Christ and disclosed by the Spirit. This flows into how the Spirit enables understanding (vv. 11–16).
original_language_note: “Mystery/hidden wisdom” (Greek: mystērion) means God’s once-hidden plan now revealed in Christ. Calling Jesus the “Lord of glory” underscores His divine majesty despite the shame of the cross.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the content of God’s hidden wisdom—crucified and now exalted as the Lord of glory. The Spirit reveals the significance of His cross for our salvation and future glory.
apply_it:
- Where do you feel pressure to chase the wisdom of the moment? How does the cross re-center you?
- Ask the Spirit to reveal more of God’s purposes in Christ. What new insight or comfort emerges?
- What hope does it give you that God prepared good for those who love Him beyond what we can imagine?

title: Spiritual Discernment and the Mind of Christ
content:
Just as only a person’s own spirit knows their inner thoughts, only the Spirit of God knows God’s thoughts. Believers have received the Spirit from God so they can understand what God has freely given in the gospel.
Paul and his co-workers teach with words taught by the Spirit, communicating spiritual truths in spiritual words. Without the Spirit, the message seems like foolishness and cannot be grasped.
Those led by the Spirit can evaluate all things rightly because they share in Christ’s perspective. Quoting Scripture, Paul concludes that while no one can instruct the Lord, believers have the mind of Christ.
context_note: This section explains how the hidden wisdom becomes known: through the Spirit’s indwelling and teaching. It prepares for chapters 3–4, where Paul addresses immaturity and divisions that contradict having the mind of Christ.
original_language_note: “Natural person” (Greek: psychikos) refers to the person operating by merely human (unspiritual) resources. “Spiritual” (pneumatikos) describes those shaped and enabled by the Holy Spirit.
jesus_connection: To have the Spirit is to share the mind of Christ. The risen Jesus pours out the Spirit so His people can understand and live the gospel He accomplished.
apply_it:
- Pray: Spirit, help me understand what You have freely given in Christ. Where do you need His clarity today?
- How might having the ‘mind of Christ’ reshape your reactions—especially in conflict or confusion?
- Where do you sense resistance to the Spirit’s teaching? Bring it honestly to God.

title: Spiritual Infancy and Factionalism
content:
Paul speaks to the Corinthians as spiritual infants, not yet ready for solid food. Their jealousy and quarrels reveal a worldly mindset. Their slogans—“I follow Paul… I follow Apollos”—show they are walking like the surrounding culture, chasing status through human leaders.
Instead of celebrating different gifts in the body, the church has turned leaders into badges of superiority. Paul’s rebuke is pastoral: spiritual maturity is not measured by cleverness or by the teacher you prefer, but by love and unity.
The call is to grow up in Christ. Milk is good for infants, but we should not remain infants. The sign of growth is leaving behind rivalry and embracing a Christ-centered identity.
context_note: This follows Paul’s earlier critique of boasting in human wisdom (1:18–31) and sets up his redefinition of ministry in 3:5–9. It prepares the way for his discussion of how we build on Christ (3:10–15).
historical_note: In Corinth’s honor-shame culture, patrons, orators, and philosophers attracted followers. Christians were tempted to treat apostles like competing philosophical schools.
original_language_note: “Worldly” (sarkikos) points to fleshly, merely human patterns. Paul contrasts this with being “spiritual” (pneumatikos)—shaped by the Spirit.
jesus_connection: Jesus gathers one flock under Himself, not under competing human names. He prayed for our unity so the world would know the Father sent Him.
apply_it:
• Where do you feel tempted to define yourself by personalities, platforms, or preferences rather than by Christ?
• What might moving from “milk” to “solid food” look like in your current season?
• How could you contribute to unity in your church this week?

title: Servants Through Whom You Believed
content:
Paul and Apollos are not rival masters but servants through whom the Corinthians believed, each assigned a role by the Lord. Paul planted the gospel seed and Apollos watered it, but only God gives the growth.
This perspective removes boasting. Planters and waterers share one purpose and will be rewarded for faithful labor, not for the outcomes only God can produce.
The church is both God’s field and God’s building. Believers belong to God, and leaders are God’s coworkers—not celebrities to be claimed, but stewards to serve the church.
context_note: Develops the correction to factionalism from 3:1–4 and transitions to the building metaphor expanded in 3:10–15.
historical_note: Apollos was an eloquent teacher from Alexandria who ministered in Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:24–28; 19:1).
original_language_note: “Servants” (diakonoi) underscores humble service. “Gives the growth” (auxanō) stresses God’s ongoing action as the true source of increase.
jesus_connection: Jesus, the Lord of the harvest, assigns roles in His mission. Our confidence rests not in gifted workers but in Christ who builds His church.
apply_it:
• Where have you confused faithful service with guaranteed results?
• How can you honor different roles in ministry without comparing or competing?
• What would it look like to pray for God’s growth rather than forcing outcomes?

title: Building on the Only Foundation
content:
By God’s grace, Paul laid a foundation like a skilled master builder: Jesus Christ. No other foundation can sustain the church. Others build on this foundation, and must take care how they build.
Paul pictures different building materials—gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw. A coming Day will reveal the quality of each person’s work. God’s testing fire will show what endures.
If the work remains, there is reward; if it burns, there is loss—yet the builder himself will be saved as through fire. Salvation is by grace, but our labor will be evaluated for faithfulness and quality.
context_note: Flows from the ‘God’s building’ image (3:9) and prepares the temple emphasis (3:16–17). It also anticipates later instructions on corporate worship and order.
original_language_note: “Foundation” (themelios) highlights what the entire structure rests on. “The Day” (hē hēmera) is shorthand for the final day of God’s judgment.
jesus_connection: Christ is the only foundation. Ministry that is truly Christian must be aligned with His person and work; what is built for His glory endures.
apply_it:
• What ‘materials’ are you using—habits and motives that will endure, or things that won’t last?
• How does knowing Christ is the foundation shape your decisions in church life and service?
• Where might God be inviting you to focus on quality, not just activity?

title: You Are God’s Temple
content:
Paul declares that the church together is God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells among them. This gives immense dignity and responsibility to the community.
Because the church is God’s holy dwelling, to tear it down through division, false teaching, or destructive behavior is deadly serious. God will defend His holy temple.
context_note: This intensifies the building image (vv. 9–15) by naming the structure: God’s temple. It underscores the gravity of divisions already addressed in the chapter.
historical_note: In both Jewish and Greco-Roman worlds, temples were sacred spaces. To defile a temple invited divine judgment.
original_language_note: “Temple” (naos) often refers to the inner sanctuary—the dwelling place of God’s presence.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the true temple in whom God dwells (John 2:19–21), and by His Spirit He makes the church His dwelling. Our unity and holiness reflect Him.
apply_it:
• How does seeing your church as God’s temple change how you speak and act toward it?
• Are there patterns in you that harm the unity or holiness of the church?
• What positive steps could build up God’s dwelling among you?

title: True Wisdom and All Things Are Yours
content:
Paul warns against self-deception: to gain God’s wisdom, we must become ‘fools’ in the world’s eyes. Worldly wisdom cannot grasp God’s ways and is exposed as futile before Him.
Therefore, stop boasting in human leaders. In Christ, ‘all things’ are yours—leaders, the world, life, death, the present, the future. You belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God. This reorders status, security, and hope.
context_note: Concludes the unit on divisions and wisdom (chs. 1–3) with Scripture citations and a doxology-like summary that centers identity in Christ.
historical_note: Paul quotes Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11 to show that Scripture has long unmasked the pretensions of human cleverness.
original_language_note: “Wise” (sophos) and “wisdom” (sophia) echo the earlier contrast between God’s wisdom in the cross and human wisdom.
jesus_connection: Jesus is God’s wisdom for us. In Him, we receive a new identity and inheritance that frees us from boasting in people.
apply_it:
• Where do you feel pressure to appear ‘wise’ by cultural standards rather than by the cross?
• What changes when you truly believe ‘all things are yours’ in Christ?
• How could you practice boasting only in the Lord this week?

title: Servants and Stewards, Not Judges
content:
Paul resets how the Corinthians should view Christian leaders: not as celebrities to champion, but as Christ’s servants and stewards entrusted with God’s mysteries. The key requirement is faithfulness, not popularity or human approval.
He refuses to be mastered by human judgments, even his own self-assessment. A clear conscience is not the same as innocence—only the Lord’s verdict finally counts. Therefore, they must hold back from premature verdicts on leaders or one another.
When the Lord comes, He will bring hidden things to light and reveal motives. True praise will come from God at that time, not from party loyalty or public opinion.
context_note: This follows Paul’s teaching against boasting in leaders (chs. 1–3). Here he specifies the right lens for viewing leaders and defers final evaluation to Christ. The rest of the chapter applies this to Corinth’s pride and Paul’s own example.
historical_note: A ‘steward’ managed a household on behalf of its owner, accountable for faithful oversight. In the ancient world, stewards answered to the master’s inspection, not to fellow servants.
original_language_note: ‘Servants’ (hypēretai) can mean assistants/under-rowers; ‘stewards’ (oikonomoi) are household managers; ‘mysteries’ (mystēria) are God’s revealed gospel truths now made known in Christ.
jesus_connection: Leaders serve Christ and steward His gospel; Jesus is the Lord who will judge hearts at His coming. The passage directs attention away from human status to Christ’s authority and final evaluation.
apply_it:
- Where are you tempted to seek human approval rather than God’s ‘well done’?
- How might waiting for the Lord’s verdict change the way you speak about other believers or leaders?
- What would faithfulness look like in the trust God has given you today?

title: Irony and the Apostolic Pattern of Suffering
content:
Paul applies this teaching to himself and Apollos so the church will not go beyond Scripture or boast in one leader over another. He asks piercing questions: everything they have is received, so why boast as if it were earned?
Using irony, he contrasts the Corinthians’ imagined status—already rich and reigning—with the apostles’ lived reality: displayed like prisoners at the end of a procession, weak, dishonored, hungry, abused, and homeless. Far from triumphalism, apostolic ministry looks like cruciform weakness.
Yet the apostles respond like Christ taught: blessing when cursed, enduring when persecuted, answering gently when slandered. The world may treat them as the ‘scum of the earth,’ but they bear faithful witness through suffering.
context_note: This section exposes the heart of Corinthian pride and resets expectations for ministry, preparing for the fatherly appeal and corrective discipline that follow.
historical_note: ‘A spectacle’ evokes prisoners in a Roman triumph, paraded last for death. Manual labor by leaders was socially despised in elite circles, intensifying the shame the apostles bore.
original_language_note: ‘Spectacle’ (theatron) highlights being publicly displayed; ‘scum’ (perikatharma) and ‘refuse’ (peripsēma) were terms for what is scraped off—images of utter contempt.
jesus_connection: The apostles’ path mirrors Jesus’ way of the cross: weakness, dishonor, and patient blessing. Their endurance points to the crucified Messiah whose power is made perfect in weakness.
apply_it:
- How does remembering that ‘all is received’ reshape your attitude toward gifts and success?
- Where might God be inviting you to embrace humble service rather than image or status?
- When mistreated, what would it mean to respond with blessing and gentleness?

title: A Father’s Appeal: Imitate My Way of Life
content:
Paul clarifies that his sharp words aim to warn, not shame. As their spiritual father through the gospel, he cares for them in a way that many guardians cannot. He urges them to imitate him—not only his teaching, but his way of life in Christ.
To help them do this, he sends Timothy, his beloved and faithful child in the Lord. Timothy will remind them of Paul’s consistent pattern of life and doctrine, the same rule he teaches in every church.
context_note: This fatherly appeal bridges from Paul’s critique of pride to his practical pastoral care, setting up correction in the next chapters.
historical_note: A ‘guardian’ (paidagōgos) was a household attendant who supervised a child’s conduct. A father’s role carried deeper responsibility, affection, and authority.
original_language_note: ‘Imitate’ (mimētēs) highlights apprenticing one’s life to a living example of the gospel.
jesus_connection: To imitate Paul is to follow his Christ-shaped life. Spiritual parenthood and imitation reflect how Jesus formed disciples—life-on-life, teaching modeled in practice.
apply_it:
- Who has been a spiritual parent to you, and how might you thank or learn from them afresh?
- In what concrete ways could your life become more ‘imitable’ in Christ this week?
- Where do you need reminding of the simple, consistent way of Jesus in doctrine and daily habits?

title: Talk or Power? Paul’s Coming Visit
content:
Some have grown arrogant, assuming Paul will not return. He plans to come, God willing, to test not their eloquence but the reality of their power. The kingdom of God is not mere words; it is the Spirit’s power at work in transformed lives.
Paul asks whether they want him to come with a rod—discipline—or with love and a gentle spirit. Their response will determine the tone of his visit.
context_note: This closes the section on true leadership and prepares for church discipline and issues of holiness addressed in chapters 5–6.
historical_note: The ‘rod’ was a common image for corrective discipline by a father or teacher in the Greco-Roman world.
original_language_note: ‘Power’ (dynamis) contrasts with mere ‘talk’ (logos), emphasizing the Spirit’s effective work over empty rhetoric.
jesus_connection: Jesus’ kingdom comes with real power—deliverance, holiness, love—not showy speech. Paul’s gentle firmness reflects the Good Shepherd who both protects and restores.
apply_it:
- Where do you see God’s power changing lives, and how could you align with that work?
- Are there areas where you rely on words or image rather than the Spirit’s power?
- If correction is needed, how can it be received or given in a spirit of love and gentleness?

title: A Scandal and a Command to Act
content:
Paul exposes a shocking case: a man is in a relationship with his father’s wife—immorality that even pagans rejected. More disturbing than the sin itself is the church’s pride when grief and action were needed.
He instructs the gathered church to act together, with the authority of the Lord Jesus, to remove the man from their fellowship. This is not vindictive but pastoral: “hand him over to Satan” describes placing him outside the church’s protective sphere so that the sinful “flesh” is brought to an end.
The aim is redemptive: that the man’s spirit might be saved on the Day of the Lord. Church discipline is love with a long view—seeking repentance, restoration, and the church’s health.
context_note: Following chapters 1–4 where Paul confronts pride and party spirit, he now addresses a concrete moral failure. This prepares for his wider teaching on holiness and relationships in chapters 5–7. The next section explains why inaction endangers the whole church.
historical_note: Roman law and common morality condemned incest (see Leviticus 18:8 for Jewish background). House-church gatherings made discipline a community act, not a private opinion.
original_language_note: “Sexual immorality” translates Greek porneia, a broad term for illicit sexual behavior. “Hand over to Satan” (paradounai tō Satana) depicts exclusion from the church’s sphere. “Flesh” (sarx) here means the sinful nature’s dominion, not the physical body per se.
jesus_connection: Jesus taught pursuing a sinning brother for restoration (Matthew 18). Paul’s process seeks the same end under Jesus’ authority: temporary exclusion toward ultimate salvation through Christ.
apply_it:
- Where might pride keep you or your church from grieving over sin and seeking restoration?
- How does viewing discipline as loving and redemptive (not punitive) change your response to church sin?
- Pray for courage to address harm truthfully and for humility to receive correction.

title: Leaven and the Passover Lamb
content:
Paul warns that their boasting is dangerous: like yeast working through dough, tolerated sin spreads through a church. Moral rot rarely stays isolated.
He calls them to become what they are: a new, unleavened batch. The reason is deeply gospel-centered—Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Because Jesus has rescued us, we live as a festival people: not with the leaven of malice and wickedness but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
context_note: This imagery explains why inaction harms the whole body and grounds the call to holiness in Christ’s saving work. The next section applies this to relationships with insiders and outsiders.
historical_note: At Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Jewish households searched for and removed all leaven, symbolizing a break from the old life of Egypt. The church inherits this moral symbolism in light of Christ.
original_language_note: “Leaven” is zymē; a little affects the whole batch (cf. Galatians 5:9). “Passover” is pascha. “Sincerity” (eilikrineia) and “truth” (alētheia) highlight transparent, faithful living.
jesus_connection: Jesus is the true Passover Lamb whose death brings deliverance from sin’s slavery. His sacrifice creates a holy people who put away the old ‘leaven’ and embody sincere, truthful lives.
apply_it:
- What ‘small’ compromises might be leaven in your life or community?
- How does remembering Christ as your Passover Lamb motivate joyful, not grudging, holiness?
- Where can you practice sincerity and truth this week—in speech, habits, or relationships?

title: Judging Inside, Not Outside
content:
Paul clarifies a misunderstanding: his earlier instruction not to associate with the sexually immoral did not mean avoiding unbelievers. To do that, you would have to leave the world altogether.
His point targets professing believers who persist in open, serious sin—sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, abusive speech, drunkenness, swindling. With such a person, the church must not even share table fellowship, signaling the seriousness of unrepentant sin and the hope of repentance.
Paul distinguishes roles: God judges those outside; the church rightly judges those inside. The Scripture-backed command stands: remove the evil person from among you.
context_note: After grounding discipline in the gospel and corporate purity, Paul clarifies boundaries for everyday relationships, protecting mission in the world and integrity in the church.
historical_note: In the ancient world, table fellowship signified acceptance and partnership. Withdrawing it from an unrepentant insider communicated a call to repent. Early Christian meals often included the Lord’s Supper, heightening the gravity.
original_language_note: “Associate” is sunanamignysthai, to mix closely with. “Reviler” is loidoros, a habitual verbal abuser. The quote “Expel the wicked man” echoes Deuteronomy’s formula for removing evil from Israel’s midst.
jesus_connection: Jesus ate with repentant sinners outside the community while calling his followers to a new way of life. The church reflects Jesus when it engages the world with mercy yet guards its fellowship with holiness.
apply_it:
- How can you be present with unbelieving neighbors without compromising holiness?
- Do you treat ongoing, unrepentant sin among believers with sober love and hopeful prayer?
- Ask God for wisdom to balance mercy toward outsiders and integrity within the church.

title: Believers and Lawsuits Before Unbelievers
content:
Paul is shocked that Christians in Corinth are dragging one another before secular courts. Their public disputes undermine the church’s witness and forget who they are: saints who will one day share in God’s judgment over the world—and even angels. If they will judge such weighty matters with Christ, surely they can handle everyday conflicts in house.
Instead of wise, Spirit-led arbitration, they choose adversarial litigation, which Paul says is a defeat in itself. Better to be wronged than to damage the family’s unity and the gospel’s reputation. The real tragedy is that some are not merely victims but perpetrators—cheating their own brothers and sisters.
context_note: After condemning toleration of serious sin in chapter 5, Paul addresses another public scandal: intrachurch lawsuits. Next, he widens the lens to kingdom inheritance and the believers’ new identity (vv. 9–11), then applies that identity to sexual ethics and the body (vv. 12–20).
historical_note: In Roman cities like Corinth, civil suits were common and often favored the wealthy and well-connected. Public hearings could be spectacles, making private church disputes a matter of public entertainment and shame.
original_language_note: The phrase "saints will judge the world" highlights identity: "saints" (Greek: hagioi) are the set-apart people of God, entrusted with wisdom to discern.
jesus_connection: Jesus teaches reconciliation and peacemaking within the community. Because He reconciled us to God at great cost, His people are called to pursue peace and justice among themselves, reflecting His character.
apply_it: Where am I tempted to win a dispute rather than seek reconciliation? Who could help mediate a conflict in a wise and prayerful way? What would it look like, in my situation, to value Christ’s reputation above personal victory?

title: From Old Life to New Identity
content:
Paul warns that persistent unrighteous living—whether sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, same-sex sexual behavior, theft, greed, drunkenness, abusive speech, or swindling—excludes people from inheriting God’s kingdom. He says, “Do not be deceived,” because the Corinthians were at risk of normalizing old patterns.
Then comes hope: “And that is what some of you were.” The gospel changes people. In Jesus’ name and by the Spirit, they were washed, sanctified, and justified—given a new status, set apart for God, and made clean. Their future inheritance rests not in their past sins but in Christ’s saving work.
context_note: This section grounds Paul’s call away from lawsuits in a bigger gospel story: believers have a new identity and destiny. It bridges to the final section, showing why Christian freedom must align with holiness in body and life (vv. 12–20).
original_language_note: “Washed” (apelousasthe), “sanctified” (hēgiasthēte), and “justified” (edikaiōthēte) underscore a decisive change by God’s action. “Sexual immorality” translates porneia, a broad term for sexual acts outside the marriage of a man and a woman.
jesus_connection: Jesus’ death and resurrection cleanse and re-create sinners. The Spirit applies this work, giving a new heart and power to live differently, making the church a living testimony of grace.
apply_it: Where might I be minimizing a sinful pattern God wants to transform? How does remembering “that is what I was” cultivate humility and compassion toward others? What fresh step could I take today in the Spirit’s power that aligns with my new identity?

title: Bodies for the Lord: Freedom, Union, and Purity
content:
Some Corinthians were saying, “Everything is permissible” and treating the body like a temporary shell, similar to food and the stomach. Paul replies: not everything is beneficial, and nothing should master us. God will raise our bodies, as He raised the Lord, so what we do in our bodies matters eternally.
Because believers are members of Christ, sexual sin is uniquely serious: it unites one body to another in a way that conflicts with union to Christ. Scripture says, “The two will become one flesh.” Therefore, flee sexual immorality. Unlike many sins, sexual sin is against one’s own body, distorting God’s design and damaging the self.
Paul crowns the argument with identity and ownership: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit; you are not your own—you were bought at a price. The right response is worshipful stewardship: glorify God with your body.
context_note: Following the identity reminder (vv. 9–11), Paul applies it to everyday ethics. This sets up later discussions on liberty and love (chs. 8–10) and on the body’s future in the resurrection (ch. 15).
historical_note: Greco-Roman culture often separated the soul from the body and normalized prostitution. Corinth’s port-city ethos reinforced permissive sexual norms, making Paul’s teaching countercultural.
original_language_note: “Temple” is naos, the sacred inner sanctuary—intensifying the body’s holiness. “Bought” (ēgorasthete) evokes marketplace purchase, highlighting Christ’s costly redemption.
jesus_connection: Jesus’ bodily resurrection and the sending of the Spirit ground the body’s dignity. His purchase price—His own life—claims our whole selves for God’s glory.
apply_it: Where might my idea of “freedom” be mastering me? What practices help me actively “flee” rather than negotiate with temptation? How can I honor the Spirit’s presence in my body this week?

title: Mutuality in Marriage and Temporary Abstinence
content:
Paul responds to a Corinthian slogan about abstinence by affirming marital sex as good within marriage. Because sexual immorality is common, each spouse should belong to the other, honoring mutual authority over their bodies.
He warns against depriving one another except by mutual consent and for a limited time of prayer, then reuniting to avoid temptation. This is pastoral wisdom, not a command.
Paul values celibacy as his own gift, yet recognizes God gives different gifts. Marriage and singleness are both honorable callings when lived unto the Lord.
context_note: Coming after warnings about sexual sin (ch. 5–6), Paul now gives positive instruction for holiness in marriage. The chapter will widen from marital counsel to broader callings and the urgency of the times.
historical_note: Some in Corinth prized asceticism, thinking total abstinence was more spiritual. Paul corrects this by upholding conjugal rights and mutuality in marriage.
original_language_note: Porneia (sexual immorality) in v.2 frames the context. Exousia (authority) in v.4 emphasizes mutual authority of husband and wife. Charisma (gift) in v.7 highlights singleness and marriage as Spirit-given capacities.
jesus_connection: Jesus honored marriage and purity and spoke of celibacy for the kingdom. Paul applies Jesus’ lordship to bodies and desires, calling believers to loving self-giving that mirrors Christ’s love.
apply_it: {"If married, how might mutual care—physical, emotional, spiritual—reflect Christlike love this week?","If single, where do you see your singleness as a Spirit-given opportunity to serve Jesus?","Where do you need wisdom to balance prayerful devotion and realistic vulnerability to temptation?"}

title: Guidance for Married, Separated, and Mixed-Believer Marriages
content:
Paul affirms singleness for the unmarried and widows, while allowing marriage when passions burn—better to marry than to be consumed by desire.
To married believers, he relays the Lord’s command: do not divorce. If separation occurs, pursue reconciliation or remain unmarried.
For believers married to unbelievers, if the unbelieving spouse is willing to stay, the believer should not initiate divorce. The unbelieving spouse and the children are relationally set apart through the believer’s presence. Yet if the unbeliever departs, the believer is not bound—God calls us to peace. Salvation outcomes remain in God’s hands.
context_note: This develops the chapter’s balance: honoring both fidelity in marriage and the real tensions of mixed-believer homes. It leads to the next principle—stay in the calling God assigned.
historical_note: In the Roman world, divorce was common and relatively easy. Some new believers wondered if conversion required leaving an unbelieving spouse. Paul counsels stability and peace.
original_language_note: Hēgiastai (has been sanctified) in v.14 means set apart in a relational sense, not automatically saved. Douloō/dedesai (bound) in vv.15, 27–39 pertains to marital bond/obligation.
jesus_connection: Paul applies Jesus’ teaching on marriage permanence with pastoral sensitivity in mixed marriages. Christ’s peace governs even painful separations.
apply_it: {"Where might pursuing peace, rather than winning an argument, honor Christ in your home?","If married to a nonbeliever, how can you practice patient, hopeful love without pressure?","Who could help you seek reconciliation or wise boundaries in a strained relationship?"}

title: Remain as You Were Called (Circumcision, Slavery, Vocation)
content:
Paul lays down a broad rule: live the life the Lord assigned when He called you. External markers—circumcision or its absence—do not define righteousness; keeping God’s commands does.
Slaves and free people alike belong to Christ. If a slave can gain freedom, good; but status does not limit true Christian identity. All were bought with a price, so do not become slaves of people.
The point: don’t scramble for status upgrades to feel spiritual. Serve Christ faithfully where you are, with the freedom the gospel provides.
context_note: After specific marriage cases, Paul zooms out to a principle for all stations of life. This frames later advice about betrothals and widowhood with contentment and calling.
historical_note: Corinth prized status. Roman slavery varied widely; some slaves held skilled posts and could be freed. Jewish-Gentile tensions also made circumcision a hot-button identity marker.
original_language_note: Kaleō/klesis (call/calling) stresses God’s summons into Christ. Agorazō (bought) recalls redemption language (v.23). Doulos (slave) highlights belonging to Christ above all earthly ties.
jesus_connection: Jesus’ redemption sets our worth. Because He bought us with His blood, no earthly status defines or confines our service to Him.
apply_it: {"Where do you feel pressure to change status to feel significant? How does Christ’s purchase of you speak into that?","What would faithfulness look like in your present responsibilities this week?","Is there an open door to greater freedom? Ask for wisdom to pursue it without chasing identity."}

title: Virgins and the Present Crisis
content:
Without a direct command from Jesus, Paul gives trustworthy counsel: because of a present crisis, it is good to remain as you are—married or single. Marriage is good, yet it brings real-world troubles; Paul wants to spare believers unnecessary distress.
He urges an eternal perspective: the time is short and this world’s form is passing away. Therefore, hold even good things—marriage, grief, joy, possessions—lightly, using them without being mastered by them.
context_note: This section builds on the calling principle and anticipates the focus on undivided devotion. The ‘present crisis’ likely shaped pastoral counsel in Corinth’s moment.
historical_note: The ‘present crisis’ may refer to local hardship, famine, persecution, or social instability in the mid-first century, which could make new marriages especially difficult.
original_language_note: Anagkē (necessity/crisis) in v.26 frames the counsel. Schēma (form) in v.31 highlights the transient pattern of the current world order.
jesus_connection: Jesus announced the in-breaking kingdom and taught storing treasure in heaven. Paul echoes this urgent, kingdom-first mindset in practical choices.
apply_it: {"How might an eternal perspective reshape how you hold marriage, work, or possessions?","Are current pressures making big life changes unwise right now? Ask the Lord for peace and timing.","What would it mean to use the world’s goods without being owned by them?"}

title: Undivided Devotion: Concerns of Single and Married
content:
Paul wants believers free from anxieties that pull them away from the Lord. Marriage brings legitimate concerns—pleasing a spouse and tending to household affairs—while singleness can allow a more focused devotion to the Lord in body and spirit.
He isn’t restricting anyone; he offers wisdom that promotes what is fitting and fosters undistracted devotion to Christ.
context_note: This explains why Paul commends singleness in this chapter: not as superior righteousness, but as strategic freedom for mission and worship.
original_language_note: Merimna (concern/anxiety) in vv.32–34 contrasts with undivided devotion (euprosedron, v.35), portraying focus vs. fragmentation.
jesus_connection: Jesus invited disciples to seek first God’s kingdom. Paul shows how marital status can affect that pursuit and invites all to prioritize Christ.
apply_it: {"If single, where could you joyfully invest your extra flexibility for the Lord’s work?","If married, how might you and your spouse support each other’s devotion to Jesus?","What one distraction could you lay down to be more attentive to Christ?"}

title: Betrothal Decisions
content:
Paul addresses engaged couples (or guardians arranging marriages). If a couple believes they should marry, they are free to do so without sin. If a man is firmly resolved to postpone or forego marriage and both are at peace, that is also good.
In short: marriage is good; voluntary celibacy for kingdom purposes can be even better. The choice should arise from conviction, self-control, and mutual honor, not pressure.
context_note: This applies the earlier principles—calling, crisis, and devotion—to a sensitive decision many faced in Corinth.
historical_note: First-century betrothals involved family and social expectations; delays could cause pressure or shame. Paul releases believers from such pressures with gospel freedom.
original_language_note: Exousia (authority/control) and krateō (to have control) in v.37 stress mature self-governance, not compulsion.
jesus_connection: Jesus dignified both marriage and voluntary singleness for the kingdom. Paul invites decisions that maximize fruitful devotion to Christ.
apply_it: {"If discerning marriage, what motives—fear, pressure, or faith—are shaping your decision?","How can you honor the other person’s good before God, whatever you choose?","Who could pray with you for clarity and peace in timing?"}

title: Widowhood and Remarriage in the Lord
content:
Marriage is a lifelong bond; death releases a spouse to remarry. A widow is free to marry anyone, provided he belongs to the Lord. Paul’s judgment is that she may be happier remaining single, but this is Spirit-guided counsel, not a command.
The guiding principle remains: freedom in Christ used for devotion to Christ.
context_note: This closing returns to permanence in marriage and freedom in singleness, bracketing the chapter with balance and pastoral care.
historical_note: In Roman society, widows often remarried for social and economic stability. Paul affirms that Christian remarriage should be ‘in the Lord.’
original_language_note: En Kyriō (in the Lord) in v.39 limits remarriage to a fellow believer, aligning the household with Christ’s lordship.
jesus_connection: Because Jesus is Lord over life and home, even remarriage is shaped by His rule and the hope of the kingdom.
apply_it: {"If widowed or single again, what would ‘in the Lord’ look like for your next steps?","Where do you sense the Spirit’s gentle wisdom—freedom to remarry or freedom to remain single?","How can your community support you in discernment without pressure?"}

title: Knowledge vs. Love
content:
Paul begins by acknowledging the debate about food offered to idols and the claim that “we all have knowledge.” He warns that knowledge can inflate pride, while love strengthens people. The measure of maturity is not information but edification.
He adds a humbling truth: the person who thinks he has fully grasped the matter likely hasn’t. What truly matters is loving God—and those who love God are known by God. Being known by God is the deepest security and the true goal behind ethical questions.
context_note: This follows Paul’s call to consider others in matters of marriage and calling (ch. 7). It introduces the guiding principle for chapters 8–10: love directs freedom.
historical_note: In Corinth, meat often came from temple sacrifices and was sold in markets or served at banquets linked to guilds and social status. Participation raised questions about loyalty to Christ and witness to others.
original_language_note: “Knowledge” (gnōsis) contrasts with “love” (agapē). To be “known by God” echoes covenantal relationship, not mere data.
jesus_connection: Jesus embodies love that builds up—he uses his authority to serve and save. Following him means valuing people over proving we’re right.
apply_it: {"Where might being ‘right’ be more important to you than building someone up?","How does being ‘known by God’ steady you when ethical choices feel complex?","Whose faith could be strengthened by your patient love this week?"}

title: One God and One Lord
content:
Paul affirms that idols are nothing and that there is only one God. Though many speak of ‘gods’ and ‘lords,’ Christians confess a different reality.
He then gives a compact creed: one God, the Father—from whom are all things and for whom we exist; and one Lord, Jesus Christ—through whom are all things and through whom we exist. This anchors ethics in worship: who God is shapes what we do.
context_note: Paul grounds the debate in theology before returning to practical conscience issues. Right doctrine supports right love.
historical_note: Greco-Roman cities honored many deities tied to trade, crops, and civic life. Public meals often invoked these gods, making abstaining socially costly.
original_language_note: The confession re-echoes the Shema (Deut 6:4) while including Jesus as ‘Lord’ (Kyrios), the divine title used for Israel’s God in the Greek Scriptures.
jesus_connection: Jesus is confessed as Lord through whom creation came and by whom believers live. Our allegiance to him relativizes all rival ‘lords’ and guides choices about idolatrous settings.
apply_it: {"How does confessing ‘one God, one Lord’ clarify your daily decisions?","What modern ‘lords’ compete for your loyalty—status, success, approval?","How might worship reshape your use of freedom?"}

title: Freedom, Conscience, and Love’s Restraint
content:
Paul recognizes that not all believers share the same settled understanding. Some, shaped by past idol worship, still experience defilement if they eat such meat, even though food neither commends nor separates us from God.
Therefore, those with ‘strong’ knowledge must take care that their freedom does not trip up the ‘weak.’ If a knowledgeable believer eats in a temple setting and a weaker Christian follows their example against conscience, the latter is wounded. To injure a brother or sister for whom Christ died is to sin against Christ himself. Paul concludes with a personal resolve: he would gladly forgo meat forever rather than cause another to fall.
context_note: This applies the love-over-knowledge principle to a concrete scenario. It anticipates Paul’s fuller warnings about idolatry and shared worship in 1 Corinthians 10.
historical_note: Invitations to temple banquets were tied to business networks and family events. Declining could mean social loss; attending could blur lines with idol feasts.
original_language_note: “Conscience” (syneidēsis) refers to moral awareness shaped by past formation. “Stumbling block” (proskomma) pictures an obstacle that trips someone’s faith-journey.
jesus_connection: Jesus laid down his rights for the weak. Choosing restraint for another’s good imitates his cross-shaped love.
apply_it: {"Where might exercising your freedom pressure someone else to violate their conscience?","What costly restraint could protect a newer believer near you?","How does remembering ‘for whom Christ died’ change the way you view other Christians?"}

title: Paul’s Apostolic Rights Asserted
content:
Paul opens with rapid-fire questions to reassert his genuine apostleship: he has seen the risen Lord, and the Corinthian church itself is proof of his ministry. Even if some elsewhere doubt him, the Corinthians are the seal on his commission.
He then names a key issue: gospel workers have a right to basic material support, including the freedom to travel with a believing wife, as other apostles did. Paul and Barnabas, however, are portrayed as exceptions—choosing to work with their hands—raising the question of why they did so.
context_note: This follows chapter 8’s call to limit personal freedoms out of love. Here Paul models that principle: he has rights but often lays them down. The section sets up the biblical case (vv. 7–14) and his strategic choice not to use his rights (vv. 15–18).
historical_note: In the Greco-Roman world, philosophers and religious teachers often received patronage. Apostles like Peter were known to travel with spouses. Corinth, a patronage-heavy city, could easily confuse gospel ministry with status-seeking.
original_language_note: Paul repeatedly uses exousia (“right/authority”) to stress legitimate entitlement, not mere preference.
jesus_connection: Jesus commissioned apostles as witnesses of his resurrection and sent them with authority. Paul’s authority and restraint mirror Jesus’ pattern of authority used for service, not self-advancement.
apply_it:
- Where do you sense a right you could gladly set aside for the spiritual good of others?
- How does remembering what Jesus has done through you (like the Corinthians as Paul’s ‘seal’) encourage you in present challenges?
- What might it look like to hold authority with a servant’s heart?

title: Biblical Basis for Ministry Support
content:
Paul argues from everyday life: soldiers, farmers, and shepherds rightly benefit from their labor. Scripture agrees—God’s law about not muzzling an ox while it treads grain shows God’s concern that workers share in the fruit of their work.
If priests in the temple share in offerings, how much more should gospel preachers receive material support? Jesus himself ordained that those who proclaim the gospel can live from it. Paul’s point is not greed but a principle: spiritual sowing ordinarily warrants material reaping.
context_note: This strengthens Paul’s claim to rights before he explains why he voluntarily refuses them in Corinth (vv. 15–18). It also balances chapter 8 by showing that Christian love doesn’t deny legitimate support to God’s servants.
historical_note: Deuteronomy’s farming law protected draft animals and the laborer’s dignity. Jewish priests were provided for through offerings. Early Christian missionaries often relied on hospitality and gifts amidst travel.
original_language_note: The citation ‘Do not muzzle an ox’ (Deut 25:4) is used typologically. Paul’s use of ‘the Lord has prescribed’ likely echoes Jesus’ teaching about laborers being worthy of their wages.
jesus_connection: Jesus sent out workers with the expectation of care from those they served. Honoring this pattern supports the spread of his gospel and the well-being of those he sends.
apply_it:
- How can you honor those who serve you spiritually without turning ministry into a transaction?
- What does it look like to receive or give support in a way that advances the gospel, not status or control?
- Where might you need to affirm healthy, biblical expectations for church workers?

title: Choosing Not to Use His Rights
content:
After establishing his rights, Paul surprises the reader: he has not used them. He is compelled to preach; it is a trust from God, not a platform for boasting. His joy is to offer the gospel free of charge so nothing blocks its advance in Corinth.
By refusing support there, Paul removes any suspicion that he is peddling the message. His ‘reward’ is the privilege of preaching without burdening hearers, demonstrating that the gospel creates givers, not takers.
context_note: This models the love-first ethic from chapter 8 and prepares for his missionary flexibility in vv. 19–23. It also anticipates chapter 10’s warnings about disqualification, tying freedom to responsibility.
historical_note: In cities like Corinth, wealthy patrons could ‘own’ public speakers. Paul’s tentmaking avoided entanglement and guarded the gospel’s credibility in a patronage culture.
original_language_note: ‘Gospel’ (euangelion) highlights the good news as gift; ‘entrusted’ evokes stewardship language, stressing duty over preference.
jesus_connection: Jesus freely gave himself for our salvation. Paul’s choice to preach freely reflects the grace-nature of the gospel and removes barriers so people can see Christ, not a price tag.
apply_it:
- Are there helpful freedoms you might forgo to remove obstacles for someone to hear about Jesus?
- How does seeing ministry as stewardship (not self-expression) reshape your motives?
- Where could generosity make the gospel more believable to those watching you?

title: Becoming All Things to Win Some
content:
Though truly free, Paul makes himself a servant to all to win as many as possible. With Jews he lives like a Jew; with those under the law he honors their scruples; with Gentiles he does not impose Jewish customs—yet he remains under the law of Christ.
His adaptability is not compromise but love-informed wisdom. The aim is salvation: removing non-essential barriers so that people from every background can meet Christ.
context_note: Flowing from his refusal to demand rights, Paul shows positive, missionary flexibility. This supplies a concrete strategy for the gray areas discussed in chapters 8–10.
historical_note: First-century communities had sharp Jew–Gentile boundaries. Navigating diets, festivals, and purity customs required sensitivity to avoid giving needless offense.
original_language_note: ‘Slave/servant’ (doulos) intensifies the voluntary nature of Paul’s service. ‘Law of Christ’ frames his ethical boundary—love shaped by Jesus’ teaching.
jesus_connection: Jesus crossed cultural lines and humbled himself to serve. Paul imitates that pattern so others might share in the gospel’s blessings.
apply_it:
- Who in your life needs you to enter their world with humility and patience?
- What non-essentials could you hold loosely so the essential—Christ—shines clearly?
- Are your boundaries set by the ‘law of Christ’ (love) rather than by comfort or fear?

title: Run to Win: Discipline for an Imperishable Crown
content:
Paul pivots to athletic imagery familiar in Corinth: runners and fighters train with focus to win a perishable crown. Christians pursue an imperishable one, so our lives require purposeful effort.
Paul refuses aimless motion. He disciplines his body so that, having preached to others, he himself will not be disqualified. The gospel calls for grace-fueled self-control that keeps the finish line in view.
context_note: This concludes the chapter by grounding missionary flexibility in rigorous self-mastery. It bridges to chapter 10’s warnings from Israel’s history about falling despite great privileges.
historical_note: The Isthmian Games near Corinth awarded wreaths that quickly withered. Training demanded self-control in diet, time, and focus—imagery the Corinthians knew well.
original_language_note: ‘Self-control’ (enkrateia) and ‘disqualified’ (adokimos) evoke testing and approvedness—living so one’s life matches one’s message.
jesus_connection: Jesus perfectly ran the race set before him, enduring the cross for the joy ahead. Believers fix their eyes on him as they pursue holiness and mission with disciplined love.
apply_it:
- What distractions make your race aimless, and how could you simplify to run to win?
- Where is God inviting you into grace-fueled discipline (habits of prayer, Scripture, community)?
- How does the hope of an imperishable crown strengthen you to persevere today?

title: Israel’s Example: Privilege and Peril
content:
Paul reminds the church that Israel experienced great privileges: God’s guiding cloud, deliverance through the sea, and spiritual food and drink. He even says the rock that accompanied them was Christ—pointing to God’s saving presence with them.
Yet despite all these gifts, many fell in the wilderness under God’s judgment. Privilege without faith and obedience led to ruin.
Paul’s aim is sober hope: blessings are real, but they don’t exempt us from faithfulness. Grace calls us to loyalty.
context_note: After urging self-discipline (1 Cor 9), Paul now provides Israel’s story as a warning before applying it to idolatry and the Lord’s Supper. This sets up the contrast between true worship and pagan feasts in the next section.
historical_note: The cloud and sea recall the Exodus, when God led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 13–14). Manna and water from the rock sustained them in the wilderness (Exodus 16–17).
original_language_note: Paul speaks of Israel being “baptized into Moses,” highlighting identification with their leader; and calls the provisions “spiritual,” pointing to divine origin and purpose.
jesus_connection: Christ is the sustaining Rock who was present with God’s people. Salvation and ongoing provision come through him, calling us to respond with faith and obedience.
apply_it:
- Where have you seen God’s provision recently, and how does it invite deeper trust?
- Are there areas where you assume privilege equals immunity? How might God be calling you to vigilance?
- What would it look like to honor Christ as your daily sustenance?

title: Written for Our Warning and Hope
content:
Paul lists Israel’s sins—idolatry, sexual immorality, testing the Lord, and grumbling—and the judgments that followed. These accounts are written to warn us in this new-covenant era.
He cautions the self-confident: if you think you’re standing firm, be careful not to fall. Humility and watchfulness are safeguards.
Yet Paul finishes with hope: temptations are common, and God is faithful. He limits their power and always provides a way of escape so we can endure.
context_note: This section bridges Israel’s failures and the Corinthians’ temptations. It prepares the command to flee idolatry and the argument about the Lord’s Table (vv. 14–22).
historical_note: Paul likely alludes to the golden calf (Exodus 32), the Baal of Peor incident (Numbers 25), the fiery serpents (Numbers 21), and judgments in the wilderness (e.g., Numbers 14; 16).
original_language_note: Peirasmos can mean temptation or testing; God’s faithfulness ensures an ekbasis—an escape route—so believers can bear it.
jesus_connection: Jesus faced temptation and overcame (Matthew 4), and in him we share God’s faithful help. His presence provides the ‘escape’ that enables endurance.
apply_it:
- Where are you most tempted to be overconfident spiritually?
- What practical ‘escape routes’ has God already placed in your life?
- How might humility open you to God’s faithful help today?

title: The Lord’s Table vs. Idols
content:
Paul urges: flee from idolatry. He appeals to the Corinthians’ reason by pointing to the Lord’s Supper—our shared cup and bread signify real participation (koinonia) in Christ’s blood and body, making us one body.
He then compares Israel’s altar-participants with pagan sacrifices: food offered to idols is not neutral worship. Behind idols stand demons; believers must not share the Lord’s table and the table of demons.
Trying to split loyalty provokes the Lord to jealousy. We are not stronger than God; we must give him our undivided worship.
context_note: Flowing from the warning, Paul applies it to Corinth’s idol-feasts in temples. This sharp contrast prepares the nuanced conscience guidance that follows regarding marketplace meat.
historical_note: In Corinth, many social events took place in temple dining rooms where meat had been offered to idols. Participation often implied honoring the deity associated with the feast.
original_language_note: Koinonia means participation or sharing; daimonia (demons) underscores the spiritual reality behind idol worship; eidōlothuton refers to idol-offered food.
jesus_connection: The Supper centers on Jesus’ self-giving death. Because we share in him, our worship can’t be mixed with rival allegiances.
apply_it:
- What modern ‘tables’ compete for your loyalty—habits, communities, or identities that pull your heart from Christ?
- How does the Lord’s Supper shape your sense of unity with other believers?
- Where might you need to ‘flee,’ not negotiate?

title: Conscience, Freedom, and Neighbor Love
content:
Paul quotes a Corinthian slogan—“Everything is permissible”—and responds: not everything is beneficial or edifying. Christian freedom must seek the good of others.
He permits eating meat sold in markets without interrogation, since the earth is the Lord’s. At a non-believer’s table, eat what’s served without anxious questions.
But if someone flags the food as idol-offered, abstain—for their conscience’s sake. Your liberty is real, yet love willingly limits itself to help another.
context_note: This follows the absolute ban on idol feasts by addressing everyday scenarios. It anticipates Paul’s broader principle of love over rights developed throughout the letter.
historical_note: Meat from temple sacrifices often entered public markets, making scruples about its origin a common social issue for early Christians.
original_language_note: Syneidēsis (conscience) refers to moral awareness. Paul’s use of exousia (freedom/authority) is balanced by oikodomē (edification).
jesus_connection: Jesus used his freedom to serve and save others. Following him means valuing people over preferences.
apply_it:
- Where could your freedom become someone else’s stumbling block?
- How can gratitude to God guide your everyday eating, drinking, and hosting?
- What does loving restraint look like in your community?

title: Do All for God’s Glory
content:
Paul gives the sweeping principle: whether you eat or drink, do everything for God’s glory. Everyday acts become worship when directed to him.
He urges them not to cause offense to Jews, Greeks, or the church of God. Like Paul, we seek others’ good so that many might be saved.
This is freedom’s aim: God’s honor and our neighbor’s eternal good.
context_note: This conclusion summarizes chapters 8–10: liberty is real, but love and God’s glory govern its use. It also transitions into 1 Corinthians 11’s concerns about gathered worship.
original_language_note: Doxa (glory) emphasizes God’s honor and reputation. The tri-fold group—Jews, Greeks, church—covers all audiences the Corinthians might influence.
jesus_connection: Jesus perfectly sought the Father’s glory and the salvation of many. We imitate him by prioritizing God’s honor and others’ good in ordinary choices.
apply_it:
- What is one routine habit you can consciously aim at God’s glory this week?
- Who might be watching your example, and how can you remove a potential stumbling block?
- How does evangelistic love reshape your use of personal rights?

title: Imitate Christ; Headship, Honor, and Head Coverings
content:
Paul begins by urging the church to imitate him as he imitates Christ. He then teaches about relationships in worship: Christ is the head of every man, man is the head of woman, and God is the head of Christ. His concern is that prayer and prophecy be offered in ways that honor God and avoid public shame.
He addresses head coverings and hair as signals of honor in Corinth. Men should not cover their heads when praying or prophesying; women should have an appropriate covering. Paul grounds this in creation (man and woman’s origin and purpose) while also insisting on mutual dependence: in the Lord, men and women need each other, and everything comes from God.
Paul appeals to local sense of propriety and to church-wide practice to avoid quarrels. The heart issue is not fabric or hair length itself but honoring God’s order, guarding the church’s reputation, and expressing fitting humility and respect in gathered worship.
context_note: This follows chapters on conscience and freedom (chs. 8–10). Here Paul turns to corporate worship practices. It leads into more on gatherings, spiritual gifts, and order (chs. 12–14).
historical_note: In the Greco-Roman world, head coverings and hairstyles signaled honor, modesty, marital status, and social decorum. Corinth’s mixed house churches needed visible cues to avoid scandal and to respect communal norms.
original_language_note: “Head” (Greek: kephalē) can signify authority and/or source; Paul uses it to speak of relational order without denying mutuality (vv. 11–12). “Traditions” (paradosis) refers to apostolic teachings passed on to the churches.
jesus_connection: Paul’s pattern is Christlike self-giving. Jesus honored the Father’s will; worship that reflects his humility and order points to him as Lord of the church.
apply_it: Where might my worship practices draw attention to me rather than honor God? How can I show respect and mutual care for men and women in my church’s context? What cultural signals today help or hinder our witness in gathered worship?

title: Abuses at the Lord’s Supper
content:
Paul rebukes the Corinthians because their meetings do more harm than good. Social divisions surface at the meal: some eat and drink excessively while others go hungry. Such behavior despises God’s church and shames the poor.
He reminds them that ordinary hunger belongs at home. The Lord’s Supper is not a private feast but a shared act of worship. Their selfishness distorts the gospel sign of unity and love that communion is meant to display.
context_note: This rebuke prepares for the corrective: Jesus’ own words about the Supper (vv. 23–26) and a sober call to examine themselves (vv. 27–34).
historical_note: Early Christians met in homes for a shared meal (a love feast) alongside the Eucharist. In stratified Roman society, wealthier members could arrive early with better food, creating class-based divisions.
jesus_connection: The selfish meal contradicts Jesus’ self-giving. The Supper must reflect his love that includes the least and serves others.
apply_it: Do my habits at church include or exclude others, especially those with less? How can our gatherings make the vulnerable feel honored? Where might convenience be replacing love in our communal life?

title: Institution of the Lord’s Supper
content:
Paul passes on what he received: on the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread and cup, giving thanks and declaring them signs of his body and blood of the new covenant. Believers are to eat and drink in remembrance of him.
Every celebration of the Supper proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes. It is a gospel sermon in action—remembering Christ’s sacrifice, participating in its benefits, and anticipating his return.
context_note: Placed between rebuke (vv. 17–22) and warnings (vv. 27–34), these words center the church on Jesus as the meaning of the meal.
historical_note: Covenants in Scripture are ratified with blood. Jesus frames his death as establishing the promised new covenant, drawing on Passover themes of deliverance.
original_language_note: “New covenant” echoes Jeremiah 31. “Proclaim” (katangellō) highlights that the Supper publicly announces Christ’s death as good news.
jesus_connection: Direct: Jesus institutes the Supper as the sign of his atoning death and the promise of his return. The bread and cup point to the cross and the new covenant in his blood.
apply_it: When I take the Supper, what about Jesus’ death am I remembering with gratitude today? How does communion fuel my hope that he is coming again? Who might I reconcile with before sharing this meal?

title: Examining Ourselves and Waiting for One Another
content:
Because the Supper proclaims Christ’s death, to eat and drink in an unworthy manner is to sin against the body and blood of the Lord. Paul calls for self-examination and discernment of the body. Some in Corinth have experienced weakness and sickness as divine discipline for treating the meal lightly and ignoring the church’s unity.
The remedy is simple and loving: judge ourselves rightly, receive the Lord’s correction, wait for one another, and, if hungry, eat at home. When the church gathers with reverence, unity, and patience, the Supper becomes a means of grace rather than judgment.
context_note: These instructions conclude Paul’s correction about the Supper and transition toward broader teaching on orderly worship and spiritual gifts (chs. 12–14).
historical_note: House-church timing and seating could privilege the elite; waiting for one another ensured a truly shared meal and equal participation.
original_language_note: “Unworthy manner” (anaxiōs) describes how one partakes, not a person’s intrinsic worth. “Recognizing the body” (to sōma) likely includes discerning both Christ’s body in the elements and the church as his body (cf. 10:17; ch. 12).
jesus_connection: Jesus disciplines those he loves so they share his holiness. Examining ourselves leads us back to his cross and to loving his body, the church.
apply_it: Before communion, what do I need to bring into the light before Jesus? How can I practically ‘wait for’ and include others in my church family? Where is the Lord’s loving discipline inviting me to change?

title: True Spirituality: Confessing Jesus as Lord
content:
Paul begins by correcting misunderstandings about spiritual matters. The Corinthians had past experiences with pagan worship that featured dramatic spirituality but could not speak the truth about God.
Real spirituality is tested first by confession: the Holy Spirit moves people to honor Jesus as Lord, never to curse Him. The mark of the Spirit is not spectacle but allegiance to Jesus.
This sets the tone for the whole chapter: gifts are real, but they are measured by whether they serve Jesus’ lordship and build up His people.
context_note: Coming from chapters 8–11 where pride and disorder harmed the church’s unity, Paul now addresses disorder around gifts (12–14). He begins with discernment (12:1–3), then explains the Spirit’s diverse gifts (12:4–11), the body metaphor (12:12–26), and ordered roles and priorities (12:27–31), leading to love (ch. 13).
historical_note: Corinth was full of pagan temples and ecstatic religious experiences. Some Corinthian believers likely associated spiritual power with dramatic speech, making discernment vital.
original_language_note: “Spiritual gifts” (Greek: pneumatikōn) can mean “spiritual things/persons.” The confession “Jesus is Lord” (Kyrios Iēsous) is the Spirit’s work. “Cursed” (anathema) signals total rejection—impossible for someone speaking by the Spirit.
jesus_connection: The Holy Spirit’s central work is to glorify Jesus as Lord. Any true experience of the Spirit brings people under Jesus’ rule and into His saving confession.
apply_it:
- Where do you tend to equate spirituality with outward impressiveness rather than devotion to Jesus?
- How does confessing “Jesus is Lord” shape your daily decisions?
- Ask the Spirit to help you discern what truly honors Jesus in your church life.

title: Many Gifts, One Spirit, One Purpose
content:
Paul lists various gifts but anchors them in the one Triune God—Spirit, Lord, and God—who is behind them all. Diversity is not a threat; it is God’s design.
The purpose of every gift is the common good. Wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discerning spirits, tongues, and interpretation are different ways the same Spirit blesses the church.
The Spirit sovereignly distributes gifts as He wills. Gifts are not badges of status but tools given by grace to serve others.
context_note: After clarifying the Spirit’s true test (vv. 1–3), Paul catalogs gifts to correct envy and superiority. This prepares for the body metaphor (vv. 12–26) that rebukes comparison and independence.
historical_note: In Corinth, some prized tongues and public displays. Paul values all gifts but insists their aim is communal benefit, not individual prestige.
original_language_note: “Gifts” (charismata) highlights grace; “ministries” (diakoniai) underscores service; “workings” (energēmata) points to God’s power at work. The refrain “the same Spirit/Lord/God” emphasizes unity amid variety.
jesus_connection: The gifts express Jesus’ ongoing ministry to His body through the Spirit—teaching, healing, guiding, and strengthening His people.
apply_it:
- Which gifts in others do you quietly devalue or envy? How could you celebrate them for the common good?
- Where might God be inviting you to serve, even if unseen?
- Pray for the Spirit to use your gifts to meet specific needs in your church this week.

title: One Body, Many Members
content:
Paul pictures the church as a human body: many different parts forming one living whole. By one Spirit we were baptized into one body and drink of the same Spirit—erasing barriers of ethnicity and social status.
Comparison and self-pity (“I don’t belong”) or superiority and dismissal (“I don’t need you”) have no place. God arranged each member by design.
Seemingly weaker or less honorable parts are indispensable and receive special care. True unity shares pain and joy; the whole body suffers or rejoices together.
context_note: This metaphor answers Corinthian division by affirming each person’s God-given value and necessity. It bridges from gift lists (vv. 4–11) to ordered church roles (vv. 27–31).
historical_note: Ancient Corinth had sharp social ranks. The gospel subverts such hierarchies by honoring hidden members and binding all together.
original_language_note: “Body” (sōma) and “members/parts” (melē) stress organic unity. God “arranged” (ethēken) each part—intentional placement, not accident.
jesus_connection: Believers are Christ’s body—He is the head who unites and animates every part. Caring for each member reflects Christ’s own care for His people.
apply_it:
- Who in your church feels unseen? How might you show them greater honor this week?
- Where have you said, “I don’t need them”? Bring that to Jesus and ask for His love.
- When another believer suffers or is honored, how can you enter in with empathy or joy?

title: Appointed Roles and the Greater Way
content:
Paul applies the body image: the Corinthians are Christ’s body, and each is a necessary member. God has appointed various roles—apostles, prophets, teachers, miracle-workers, healers, helpers, administrators, and tongues.
Not everyone has the same role or gift. The rhetorical questions press humility and contentment. Diversity is by God’s design, not human ranking.
Paul urges them to desire the greater gifts—those most beneficial for building up the body—and then points to “the most excellent way,” preparing for love as the supreme measure in chapter 13.
context_note: This section sums up chapter 12 and transitions to chapter 13 on love and chapter 14 on orderly worship, where edification becomes the guiding principle for evaluating gifts.
historical_note: “Helps” and “administrations” likely refer to hands-on assistance and steering/leadership functions that kept early congregations healthy, not just platform ministries.
original_language_note: “Helps” (antilēmpseis) suggests supportive assistance; “administrations” (kybernēseis) evokes steering a ship—guiding leadership. “The most excellent way” (hyperbolēn hodon) points to love’s surpassing path.
jesus_connection: Jesus gives leaders and gifts to His church for her maturity. The greater way of love mirrors Jesus’ own self-giving, the ultimate pattern for all ministry.
apply_it:
- Which roles or gifts in your church do you undervalue? How could you express gratitude for them?
- What would it look like for you to “desire the greater gifts” in a way that serves others, not self?
- Ask Jesus to root your service in love that builds up the body.

title: Gifts Without Love Are Empty
content:
Paul imagines the most impressive spiritual experiences—speaking in the tongues of men and angels, profound prophecy and knowledge, mountain-moving faith, and even extreme generosity and self-giving. Then he delivers the shock: without love, these amount to noise, nothing, and no gain.
He is not dismissing gifts or sacrifice; he is reordering values. Love is not one gift among many; it is the necessary atmosphere in which every gift must operate. It is the difference between sounding impressive and being truly Christlike.
This exposes motives. Serving, speaking, giving, even suffering can be self-centered. Love seeks the good of others for God’s glory. Without it, spiritual activity becomes empty performance.
context_note: This follows chapter 12’s celebration of diverse gifts in one body and sets up chapter 14’s guidance on tongues and prophecy. Chapter 13 is the bridge: it shows the way in which all gifts must function—love.
historical_note: In Corinth, public speech and displays of status were prized. Some likely valued conspicuous gifts (like tongues) as signs of superiority, fueling rivalry.
